# Top 5 posts from r/moviecritic day

## 1. Digger will 100% become a “misunderstood at the time” cult classic - do yourself a favor and see it before it is rushed off the screen

**Score:** 1130
**Body:** I’m not saying the movie is perfect (personally my pet peeves are towards the final act). But my word, what a brilliant film!

There is no question this is Tom Cruise’s best performance of his career (he should 100% get nominated for it, and so far, he’d be my pick this year). His delivery is grandiose and grotesque, his charisma absolutely undeniable, and yes, that parliament scene is bonafide “great scenes of cinema history”.

John Goodman also delivers an incredible, Oscar worthy performance. This is one of the great roles of his career, and this is no small feat for an actor of his caliber.

Special mention to Riz Ahmed as well, whose voice of reason is absolutely pitch perfect. I only wish his character was given a proper send-off - but that’s on the writing.

The only actress that didn’t really land, weirdly enough, was Sandra Huller - whom I consider one of the best actresses of the moment. I don’t know, I think they tried too hard to make her the “younger sister”, and there was something a tad too forced about her acting this time.

Whether you like the movie or not, so many great performances are a first sign you’re watching something special. And Digger is undeniably special.

The production design is sublime - playing with its setting (which I won’t spoil) with absolute glee and a sense of effortlessness.

The photography is absolutely gorgeous, the music is both dramatic and restrained, and the choreography of it all is pure art.

Most important of all, it’s an extremely worthwhile addition to the canon of political and environmental satire. Inevitably, some people will complain about certain things being trite or trivial, but this is inevitable when tackling one of the most covered and (sadly) polarizing topics of our time. Digger goes deeper than we think, taking the side of levity when things are dark, and pure darkness when things seem fine. It’s not meant as a dissertation on climate change, but rather as a time capsule of 21st century hubris - and our needs as humans, actors and spectators. 

Many describe it (rightfully) as Dr Strangelove meets Don’t Look Up. I’d add a touch of There Will Be Blood (not because of the oil, but because of the misanthropic brutalism of its oil man, and the fact it is, ultimately, an exploration of power and human nature - more than it is about climate or oil itself). It is definitely a movie that benefited from Birdman, and its unique approach to storytelling, unsettling at first, makes sure the movie lands as a one/two punch that knocks you out.

Digger isn’t the biggest bomb in Hollywood history: it’s the most undeserved bomb in history. It is most definitely going to end up on many lists of films that were not understood when they came out. And if you love cinema, I’d say there is a good chance you’ll kick yourself for having missed it when it came out.

My advice: you may not like it the way I did, but you won’t regret giving this oddity a chance. Rush before it’s too late. Unfortunately, like its subject matter, it’s running out of time…

# Top 5 posts from r/TrueFilm day

## 1. I don’t understand some criticisms of Digger

**Score:** 37
**Body:** 
Digger amazed me. I went in without knowing anything, and I don’t know the last time a movie managed to change my perspectives and surprise me like this. 

I also read and heard many criticisms later, and I want to comment on the one I find the most bizarre. 

But first an overview of common problems people seem to have with it. Anything related to people’s dislike for Tom Cruise or his involvement with a movie like this doesn’t interest me too much. I don’t care about his personal life and find him to be an excellent actor, like Digger clearly showed. Overall there isn’t much to discuss here, if you just can’t watch Tom Cruise that’s fine but that also means you don’t have anything to say about Digger. 

Second criticism is also something I can’t really debate, and that’s the fact that some people just didn’t like the experience. Either because the first part (satire) was too corny to them, and even if that was the point, it still wasn’t pleasant to watch; or because the second part (meta commentary) took them out of the movie where they could no longer care about the satire plot or had a good reason to care about the meta/ making the play plot either yet. Or because it looked ugly, and again, even if that is on purpose, it doesn’t make it pleasant. Those are the basic things I saw mentioned a lot. 

Personally, I totally enjoyed the satire part for itself and was immersed in the story. When the meta segment took place, it made me curious to see where it’s going, while still being interested in the plot of the satire play too. And I thought it all looked very cool and unique. 
But I can’t convince anyone about what they find corny, boring, or unpleasant to watch, and I agree that the awareness that something is a purposeful choice doesn’t necessarily change the experience. My experience was just the total opposite, it pulled me in from the start and then just kept being more than that. 

The third criticism is something I heard a few times and kind of annoys me, it seems more like a reaction to marketing (hiding the twists.). I heard a few people say how the big “twist” , by which they refer to the first twist that tells us the satire is actually a play, should have been known from the start, or how it was underwhelming. 
The structure of the movie clearly fits into three parts, the reveal of the play sets the second part in motion, and I am surprised by how many times people who talk about their disappointment with this twist totally forget to even mention that this sets the stage for the second twist that leads to the third part of the movie. For me, the first reveal had an interesting destabilizing effect where I realized there was more to what I thought I was watching, but the second reveal was the real shock and put everything in place. 

So I am not sure why anyone would think that changing this flow would have been better in any way, or act like the movie blew its big twist after the first 15-20 min as if the second and more important one never happened. The sequence is so clean and makes perfect sense, so I don’t get this. 

**But my biggest disconnect is with people who seem stuck on the second part of the movie as if the third one never happened. I keep seeing the movie getting accused of wanting to be a satire but removing itself from being a satire by shifting to meta commentary about satires.**

In fact it seems most posts here about this movie are super focused on what the movie says about satires and their power, or lack thereof, even implying that the movie’s main focus is commenting on Don’t Look Up or something. While obviously that commentary is an element the meta segment seems to be focused on, the movie then does the complete opposite from this perceived removal when it tells you that all the events seen in the satire actually happened. 

This completely changes all the implications. Cruise’s character now 20 years later may have issue with some parts being too much of a caricature or unrealistic, but you as viewer would think that the overall criticism is that the whole satirical play is unrealistic and exaggerated, just to learn that the actual plot, the most extreme part of it, is completely real.

And then it really doesn’t matter if Digger is a cartoonish villain, or if he was actually a bit more charismatic and refined, or if he was on a plane with the president or not, because the most outrageous elements of his life and actions aren’t even a question, they happened. 

Instead of staying in the meta space of examining satires while making a satire, the movie pulls you into a realistic drama where it clearly stands behind its story. It’s no longer a satire or a meta movie, it’s a tragedy. 

It had a profound effect on me, that final switch of perspectives. It was sad and shocking, and I really can’t remember the last time I was surprised like that. 

Even if it didn’t manage to affect you that way, I don’t get how anyone can blame it for not being brave or for hiding behind a meta satire, criticizing in a way that tries to avoid criticism etc. There’s no bigger statement it could have made then it did by declaring it was all real. It’s obviously not trying to remove itself from its message, it totally dives into it, and just in the moment when you think you get what it’s doing. 

I mean, that scene where they are debating the point and validity of the satire (and I disagree that it was done in a way that made the director seem incompetent or the satire total trash), just to hit you with the facts that everything you were watching happened, you realize as a viewer that you didn’t even understand the actual issue of pt 2. They live in the post Digger world so for them it makes sense to debate the approach the play took, but for the viewer, you basically learn that the actually important part (plot of the play) never even was a question. 

Anyway, I am not explaining anything with the post that the movie doesn’t explicitly say, and I am sure everyone who saw it got it, but that’s why I don’t get why this is what it gets shit for.

### Top 5 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. I want to rewatch it to stew on this thought I had but I feel like a lot of people are kinda taking Kenny’s speech to be “true” and I have to wonder if taking his word as the movies message isn’t… missing the message. There’s an extent to which Kenny himself is using the play to pull his own kinda digger-esque stunt of using the truth and farce to control the narrative and stay in the spotlight in some way, to stay in the conversation and feel like a benefactor, despite actively destroying everything. Most productions and tvs and movies fit into that dynamic too, where a mostly hands off overlord occasionally shows up to impose his weird preferences on something he doesn’t really understand but needs to pretend to in order to appear cultured and in control, while the actual craftspeople making the art invest their limited time and effort into making something they can all stand behind and say they believe in. Something so meaningful that adds meaning to their lives that a rich person would never understand and brush under the rug because that’s not why he commissioned the work, he just wanted to show off to his rich friends and feel better about his own complicity.
  - Kenny isnt trying, he's succeeding. The man whose family destroyed the world is rich, lives his best life, is loved by the miserable (including the "woke" actor after he finds his daughter) and faced no consequences 

All the poor people laughing at him are doing exactly what he wants them to. They find the play goofy, feel superior and go back to their shithole of a home happy. Status quo
    - My reading was more compassionate. I don’t think the audience is a bunch of assholes, I think they’re human beings enjoying art, and I think you seem contemptuous at them for having the gall to live lives in the apocalypse but to me that’s just an accurate look at reality, it’s not acidic or convicting, it’s just the complexity of society. It does have an impact like you say, but I don’t think the judgement is as callous as you claim. This movie was tragic to me but it was a lot more compassionate and understanding to me than most people are reading it.
2. For me, I really just didn’t think it was very funny. I know one could argue that’s part of the satire, but I’m probably not gonna like a movie that calls itself a comedy of catastrophic proportions not having anything funny in it. Most of the jokes are just people cursing in a funny voice. 

I’m glad people liked this movie more than me though
  - Yeah that’s my Don’t Look Up criticism in a nutshell 

It was just brutally unfunny. 

I tend to think Digger relied less on laughs to be compelling than the hunk of shit I just mentioned, but I get the criticism around it. I maybe chuckled like once or twice. I wouldn’t say I laughed a single time. 
  - Curtis agrees that none of it is funny. That's the moment the film really started working for me because I agreed with him. Then it got incredibly deep and profound.
    - I think two things are happening at once. 

Parts of Fossil Fools are funny, or at least were funny to me. Parts of it aren't very funny. Also the timing and delivery of the jokes are sometimes off, which makes it not great. But there's a core problem when it comes to relating to Fossil Fools: it's a satire about things that we have never experienced and have little knowledge about. Yes, it's similar to what we're going through, but it's not the same.  
We don't have hundreds of hours of Digger Rockwell footage in this world. We are therefore fundamentally incapable of actually relating to the satire in the play, the same way someone from Country A with very little knowledge of Country B couldn't relate well too satire from Country B outside of high level jokes and universal concepts. The movie actually places its characters in a fully realized world that excludes us, because it's a different world. 

Secondly, Curtis fundamentally doesn't want to, or in fact cannot laugh the events depicted. But this IMO is actually motivated primarily by the personal crisis he's going through, not by the quality of Fossil Fools per se. We are told, after all, that it's a cult classic that has been found funny for years—of course, this remake is bigger and different, but the audience does laugh at the end, which proves that it does work for the people of that world. But for Curtis, as he's making a satire about a cataclysmic tragedy, he's anxiously waiting to see whether he's going to find himself in a similar tragedy or not (one caused by the very events he's been hired to satirize). So he can't laugh at it no matter what, until his own anxiety can pass.

This makes the comedy difficult to approach for the real world audience, but it's a logical consequence of the story we have.
      - Goodman hitting his religious advisor in the head with a Bible while yelling "the Bible was written by Hebrews" was hilarious though
3. Criticism is for the most part being directed at “Fossil Fools” as if that were the whole movie and not merely a story within a story. And for many people that story within a story clashes with their worldview. For them the idea that this movie is about people looking back nostalgically and grieving a world they lost is An Inconvenient Truth.
4. I love your passion. I have seen the film 4x and will be going back for a 5th on Tuesday before it leaves theaters and then I can move on and watch the new Nathan Fielder one, which I am also extremely eager to see.

Digger is an uncomfortable and anxiety provoking film but life has felt that way for me and once I realized the film was holding up a mirror in front of my face, it just felt like an incredibly profound experience.

Digger moved me in a way no other film has. I was stunned that it wasn't universally seen as a masterpiece. All I can come up with is that taste is subjective and people like what they like. 

Digger is a layered experience with a lot of different themes and meanings and I like things that I can keep going back to and learning more about. 

Digger might not be for everyone, but those that love it will REALLY love it. Just ask Neil Young!


## 2. Ken Russell's The Devils (1971) – A couple of questions about the plot. (Also, go see it, it's great!)

**Score:** 6
**Body:** I just got back from *The Devils*, and I implore you to watch it on the big screen while you can. After all the moral panic and censorship this movie has incited over the years, I think audiences in 2026 are in a better position than ever to recognize what a smart, brave, transgressive yet deeply ethical work of art this is. (Only one person in my screening walked out! *In the American South!*) The new 4K transfer is immaculate—I was going to say it looks totally modern, but that's not much of a compliment considering how dim and dull most movies look nowadays in comparison. 

I could keep gushing, but I did have a couple of questions about the plot. In addition to the complex political intrigue and intentional ambiguities, I also just struggled to hear some of the dialogue because my cinema had very echoey walls.

Question 1: What did you understand to be King Louis XIII's motives in visiting Loudun? There's a great scene where Louis arrives at the abbey full of "possessed" nuns disguised as a duke and presents Father Barre with a box supposedly containing a relic of the Crucifixion. Barre uses it to "exorcise" the nuns—before Louis reveals the box is empty. Barre has a tense exchange with Louis, who openly questions whether Barre is a charlatan. As Louis leaves, the crowd jeers at Barre, and the nuns redouble their frenzy into a full-on orgy. 

At first, I thought Louis was simply there to knock Barre (and by extension Richelieu) down a peg. The film begins with Richelieu's proposal to Louis that they centralize power by uniting Church and State, but there's clearly a lot of tension between them. Louis undermining Barre could simply be a way to assert royal dominance over the inquisition. I'm wondering, though: are we supposed to think Louis intentionally provoked the nuns to a full-on orgy? This strains credulity for me a little bit, since while Barre had been carefully stage-managing the nuns up till that point, the orgy seemed too spontaneous and chaotic for anyone to have predicted. 

Question 2: (This one's a bit more straightforward.) When did Baron Laubardemont get permission to destroy the walls of Loudun? ## 5. You can see everything is disgusting and brilliant

**Score:** 0
**Body:** I got into Nathan Fielder years ago from a random video essay on Nathan For You, and somewhat naively, I never felt it was in bad taste. The most memorable characters: The Bill Gates impersonator, the private investigator, the small dick sports car guy, the guy who drinks his grandson's piss. In a sense they were kind of bad people, or at least a little deserving, and that's why it felt ok to laugh at them. And the others, my mind just kind of brushed them off because Nathan takes a lovably submissive role in any interaction. 

Then he takes the same concept and applies it to Benny and Elizabeth and I start to see a different perspective. It starts with a jeering feeling: she's a bad person and Billy is probably silly, stupid, or as bad as her for being with her. Then Nathan is talking to her father, we're laughing at how funny the interaction is, and suddenly he drops that Elizabeth was sexually assaulted. In a flash, you realize this is horrifying. We keep laughing at this whole situation but slowly the reality sets in as a family gets torn apart right in front of our eyes, and there's this perverted, voyeuristic, almost manic feeling to it that made me feel really fucking weird and disgusted.

You realize this whole situation is fucked and everyone’s been laughing like wolves. It's heartless to make fun of a woman as she's being pulled away from her family, especially if were to believe her act that shes markedly autistic and doesn’t even understand the most obvious joke of all time. And then there's the flip side, where she might be performing for us and for Nathan. Meanwhile I still felt empathy for these people, even Benny, who is revoltingly manipulative and narcissistic.

Although Nathan seemed to have walked the line quite tastefully, there’s one moment in particular that I found very gross. On the day she’s going to jail, he’s cracking sex jokes and giving her gag gifts. Does does he or Lance or any of the crew have not a shred of empathy for a family that is likely never gonna be the same again? 

The obvious devil on your shoulder is going to say, “Yeah, but she’s evil too. She defrauded people.” okay? Does dehumanizing and torturing someone become OK just because they are not your definition of a good person? This is a much more callous and deep and cutting and fucked up version of Nathan for you. 

I started to feel a little bit of hope when I saw Amanda Seyfried. She's kind, beautiful and composed in a way that almost sets you at ease. She’s right, she’s doing the right thing. The mythologically correct thing. She tries to empathize with Elizabeth, she gets into politics with Benny at the dumpling dinner, and she does everything politically and optically right. But then you start to think “Why the fuck does she look like she’s having so much fun.”

In the recreation, when Elizabeth says she gets bullied in jail because of Seyfried's show, you see a crack in Amanda’s veneer. The perfect performance fades and all of a sudden she starts grasping at reasons why Elizabeth is guilty and reveals herself to be just as opportunistic as Elizabeth or even Benny but she’s better at following the rules and presenting herself as pure and good. She had very little thought in her own effect on this person. She, just like us, thought: Elizabeth Holmes is bad so it doesn’t matter what I say about her. Kind of emblematic of how our politics feel right now. 

And then Elizabeth herself. I almost want to believe that she is the manipulative person that the entire media has portrayed her to be, because the flip side of that is so shockingly disturbingly depressing: This fucking Benny guy is just one of the many men who has been completely taking advantage of her doe eyed love and has led her like a lamb to the slaughter into this horrible mess.

I usually say I watch movies to be entertained, or to get some insight into why we do the things we do. This made me feel disgusted at the real people, the characters, the production, the audience next to me giggling, and myself for sitting there, and yet, somehow that ends up being profound and beautiful and layered. I’ve not seen art this good in a long time.
